newsitem.title: USA: SBC predicts $1 billion profit increase from merger.
newsitem.headline: SBC predicts $1 billion profit increase from merger.

text.p: Regional phone power SBC Communications Inc. predicted Thursday that its merger with Pacific Telesis Group will generate additional profit of $1 billion a year by the year 2000, surprising analysts.
"That's higher than we forecast," said analyst Bill Deatherage of brokerage Bear, Stearns & Co. Inc.
San Antonio-based SBC also said it expected to record one-time costs associated with the $16.5 billion merger, which closed April 1, of $1.9 billion to $2.3 billion.
SBC stock edged up 37.5 cents to $60.625 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

The merger with Pacific Telesis made SBC the dominant local phone company in seven Western states, including California and Texas. The company is also believed to be in talks with AT&T Corp. about a possible mega-merger that would be the biggest in U.S. corporate history.
The projected earnings increase from the Pacific Telesis merger would surpass by nearly 50 percent SBC's 1996 net income of $2.1 billion, or $3.46 a share.

"They're promising that and they're going to deliver more," said NatWest Securities Corp. analyst Bill Vogel. "I think it's obvious now that they can achieve higher growth combined than they would have on their own."

Deatherage said he was bumping up his fiscal 1998 projection from $4.05 per share to $4.10. The consensus analyst estimate for 1997 is $4.07, according to First Call, which tracks analyst predictions.
Both Deatherage and Vogel said they see SBC in a position to sustain double-digit growth -- in the 10 percent to 12 percent range -- over the long term.

SBC, which operates Southwestern Bell, Pacific Bell, Nevada Bell and the Cellular One network, said the source of the new income will come from a combination of new growth and an aggressive cost-cutting program.
Vogel said the greatest strength Pacific Telesis brings to SBC is its expertise as a cost cutter. "They really are the pioneers on that front," he said.
For instance, the company will cut its collection centers from 24 to 13, Vogel said after participating in an analysts' conference call with SBC.

The company is expecting to record a $200 million charge in the second quarter associated with worker severance stemming from the consolidations. It would not provide estimates for how many of its 114,000 workers will lose jobs. Still, the company expects to be adding about as many jobs as it cuts over the period, SBC spokesman Larry Solomon said.

In addition to layoffs and other consolidation charges, the company expects merger-related charges for scaling back of an investment in video services and the halting of construction of a hybrid fiber-coaxial network in California. State and federal regulatory action during the review of the merger were also being added to the cost, SBC said.
Also surprising to analysts was the large projected cost for the implementation of a phone number portability system for customers switching from SBC to new local competitors.

SBC said that will cost $1.5 billion on a pretax basis. It will be a drag on earnings -- $30 million in 1997's second quarter, $175 million for the year and another $350 million after 1997 -- in the near term until the Federal Communications Commission decides on a method for SBC to recoup its costs.
